source.title: Overthinking the Truth: Understanding how Language Models Process False Demonstrations
source.authors: Danny Halawi; Jean-Stanislas Denain; Jacob Steinhardt

page_placements.theme: Label-copying heads in few-shot classification ICL, and the failure modes they cause

record.tranche_reason: Tests induction-like heads in a new setting: few-shot classification with false demonstrations in pretrained language models. It does not reproduce the original repeated-token task or its training-time measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper studies false induction heads that attend to labels after same-class demonstrations and promote those labels. It does not measure the canonical [A][B] … [A] → [B] behavior, previous-token-head composition, induction-head formation during training, or token-index loss. Training-loss curves and abrupt training-time transitions are not tested. Values cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the induction-head idea to define 'false induction heads', but it measures a different construct. These heads attend to labels after same-class demonstrations and promote false labels. Its score is a class-level prefix-matching score on false few-shot prompts in pretrained LMs. It never measures token-level [A][B]…[A]→[B] copying, previous-token-head composition, small attention-only models, training dynamics, or token-index loss. Its results bear on false context-following, a related construct, not on any version as stated, so they go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but it omits the paper's first main finding. The authors find 'overthinking': accuracy with correct and incorrect demonstrations diverges at a critical layer, and early exit beats the full model on false prompts across 11 models. They also identify a few late-layer false induction heads, analogous to Olsson et al.'s induction heads, whose ablation reduces but does not remove the accuracy gap.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses logit-lens layerwise classification, prefix-matching scores, head-output logit analysis, and head ablation on false few-shot demonstrations; it does not reproduce the original repeated-token training analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The ablation effect differs by label condition and dataset: the average gap reduction is 38.98% for permuted labels, 15.14% for half-permuted labels, and 31.47% for random labels; several individual dataset results are small or reversed.

fits_no_version.finding: In GPT-J, ablating the 5 heads with the highest class-based prefix-matching scores cuts the correct-vs-incorrect accuracy gap by 38.98% (permuted labels, averaged over 14 datasets). Half-permuted gives 15.14% and random labels 31.47%. Random heads give 3.97%, -16.50% and -18.74%. Results vary by dataset, and some are reversed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Late-layer 'false induction heads' in pretrained LMs copy false labels from same-class demonstrations and cause part of false context-following.

fits_no_version.finding: The selected heads raise the permuted-label logit 6.5 more than the correct-label logit. 100 random 5-head sets average -0.04 (SD 0.41).
Class-level prefix-matching scores stay low early and rise around the critical layers. The text claims this for all models; figures show three.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Abstract (class-level) induction-like heads appear in late layers across pretrained LMs.

fits_no_version.finding: Zeroing late attention heads in GPT-J raises permuted-label calibrated accuracy from 37.42 to 47.58. This matches full late-layer ablation. Correct-label accuracy dips slightly (65.54→64.46).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Overthinking on false demonstrations is driven mainly by late attention heads rather than MLPs.

record.problems: The causal head-ablation results are for GPT-J; cross-model prefix-matching evidence is correlational. The authors state that ablations do not fully remove the accuracy gap and note zeroing head outputs may move states off-distribution. The experiments focus on text classification with many incorrect few-shot examples.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 reports dataset-specific ablation results across 14 datasets, label conditions, head selections, and two metrics; these were not exhaustively extracted. Table 2 has further selected-dataset cells and percentage changes in correct-prompt performance omitted here. Aggregate Table 3 results and several illustrative differing outcomes are retained.

untested.parts: Canonical [A][B]…[A]→[B] copying, composition with a previous-token head, and small attention-only transformers: none tested.
Training-time formation, abruptness, loss bump, timing relative to in-context learning gains.
Share of in-context learning (loss vs token index) carried by induction heads in large models.
Token-level induction heads across families and training runs. Only class-level prefix-matching is shown, as figures for three models.
Effects of training data and training setup on formation.
Which mechanism carries few-shot task learning as distinct from copying.
Sub-steps or multiple transitions during formation.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's labels were dropped. The V1 'supports' and 'limits_scope' labels apply V1 to an analogous construct (class-level false-label copying in 6B pretrained models), whereas V1 names token-level induction in small attention-only models. The V4 'supports' label rests on a correlational, figure-only class-level score, not on token-level induction behaviour. The tranche is T4-like: the study uses the induction-head concept as an analogy to pick heads and reports its own phenomenon. Figure 25 (ablating 15, 35 or 75 heads helps more) and Table 2/3 ΔTP values are unrecorded but do not bear on any version.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests an analogous false-demonstration mechanism, not canonical repeated-token completion or composition with an earlier previous-token head, and does not use small attention-only transformers.
Formation during training, abruptness, training-loss bump, and timing relative to in-context-learning gains are not measured.
The study examines incorrect few-shot classification demonstrations, not most in-context learning or later-token loss in large transformers.

Candidate false-induction-head scores are examined across studied language models, but the identified heads are causally ablated only in GPT-J. Training runs, other architectures, and modalities are not tested.
The study varies demonstration-label conditions, not training data properties or training setups that determine whether or when induction heads form.
The study does not determine what mainly carries few-shot task learning as distinct from copying repeated tokens.
The study does not measure training-time formation or test whether it comprises multiple transitions.

relation.reason: Section 5 explicitly draws on induction heads, but its class-based prefix matching and false-label ablations measure a different construct.

tranche.reason: Uses the induction-head idea to identify and ablate class-sensitive false-label heads; reports false context-following results without testing a catalog claim version.

source_check.notes: All listed values and standard errors match the source. State corrections apply to catalog claim interpretation: the reported local gap reductions and increases remain valid, but rows linked to no version cannot establish a version's effect.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: GPT-J false-demonstration classification, especially the aggregate permuted-label condition
reader_labels.reason: Selected heads promote false labels and their ablation reduces the accuracy gap; the aggregate permuted-label reduction is 38.98% (r1, r7). This supports an analogous false-induction mechanism, not the canonical repeated-token circuit.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Across label conditions and individual datasets
reader_labels.reason: The effect is incomplete and varies: the aggregate reduction is smaller for half-permuted labels, and selected datasets show little or reversed gap reduction (r2, r14, r15, r16).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Prefix-matching measurements across the evaluated language models on Unnatural
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports that prefix-matching scores rise around critical layers for all evaluated models, though numerical curves are provided only for three (r9, r10).
